title: Diagnostic accuracy and clinician-rated reasoning quality dissociate in a blinded evaluation of large language models in psychiatry
authors: Jin, K. W.; Rostam-Abadi, Y.; Chaudhary, P.; Garrett, M. A.; Huang, A. S.; Montelongo, M.; Nagpal, C.; Shei, J.; Weathers, J.; Zhang, J. S.; Sharma, M. S.; Chen, Q.; Kim, J.; Malgaroli, M.; Mathis, W. S.; Rodriguez, C. I.; Selek, S.; Pittenger, C.; Yip, S. W.; Zaboski, B. A.; Xu, H.
abstract: BackgroundEvaluations of large language models (LLMs) in medicine rest largely on diagnostic accuracy. We report what we learned evaluating four frontier LLMs on psychiatric diagnosis, where we asked whether clinician assessment of model reasoning adds information that accuracy does not. MethodsFour LLMs produced ranked five-diagnosis differentials for 196 psychiatric vignettes (135 screened published case reports; 61 unpublished, clinician-authored). An automated adjudicator scored accuracy. On a random 30-vignette subset, five psychiatrists blinded to model identity judged correctness and rated reasoning on a 0-4 rubric adapted from the ACGME Psychiatry Milestones. We validated the adjudicator against the clinicians, measured the reproducibility of accuracy across generation runs and repeated adjudication, and tested whether computable reasoning trace features could substitute for clinician ratings. ResultsOn all 196 vignettes, automated top-5 accuracy ranged from 0.759 to 0.837, and the majority verdict of three adjudication passes separated one of six model pairs. On the 30 rated vignettes, clinician-determined accuracy separated no pair, while reasoning separated five. Two systems were equally accurate (0.827 each; difference bounded within {+/-}0.059, or {+/-}0.10 after Holm adjustment) yet differed by 0.70 reasoning points (95% CI, 0.50 to 0.90). The adjudicator agreed with held-out clinician majorities less closely than individual clinicians did (0.83 to 0.85 vs 0.89 to 0.96), regeneration changed top-1 correctness for 18 of 119 pairs, and reference strings that combined several diagnoses were scored as misses until split. Trace features that tracked ratings across model averages did not track them across individual traces. ConclusionsAccuracy did not distinguish models that clinicians rated differently, and automated accuracy depended on how it was scored. Where LLMs are meant to support clinical reasoning, structured clinician assessment of reasoning belongs in pre-deployment evaluation.

infographic.key_insight: In psychiatric diagnosis, two LLMs can look equally accurate but still differ meaningfully in the quality of their reasoning, so accuracy alone can miss important model differences.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For clinical AI evaluation, this suggests clinicians should assess not just whether a model gets the right diagnosis, but how well its reasoning supports safe and trustworthy use.
method: 4 frontier LLMs generated ranked top-5 psychiatric differentials for 196 vignettes.
An automated adjudicator scored diagnostic accuracy across cases and generation runs.
Five blinded psychiatrists rated correctness and reasoning on 30 vignettes using a 0–4 rubric.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the 30 clinician-rated vignettes, accuracy separated no model pair, but reasoning separated five pairs; one equally accurate pair differed by 0.70 reasoning points.
infographic.watch_item: Automated accuracy depended on adjudication details and was less aligned with clinician judgment than clinician-to-clinician agreement, so implementation should not rely on accuracy-only benchmarking.
infographic.paper_title: Diagnostic accuracy and clinician-rated reasoning quality dissociate in a blinded evaluation of large language models in psychiatry

title: Efficiency of a Multi-step Screening and Enrichment Process for Prospective Sepsis Cohort Enrollment
authors: Cosimi, L. A.; Qi, W.; Naz-McLean, S.; Pan, K.; Li, S.; Laibinis, H. H.; Rooney, A. R.; Moran, C.; Valentine, G. C.; Hwang, S.; Deguine, J.; Pickard, J.; Hung, D. T.; Woolley, A. E.
abstract: BackgroundHost response and biomarker research to advance sepsis therapeutics requires well-characterized cohorts with longitudinal biospecimens across a range of hosts and infections. Automated screening based on SIRS criteria is sensitive but nonspecific and identifies more candidates than research teams can approach, sample, and follow longitudinally. We evaluated a structured enrichment review by non-physician study staff, done after automated screening in a hospital-wide prospective sepsis cohort. MethodsThe CISID cohort is a prospective observational study of hospitalized patients with suspected sepsis, enrolling adults from the ED, inpatient wards, and ICUs at a tertiary academic medical center. Patients were identified through: (1) automated electronic health record screening for two or more SIRS criteria with a 24-hour lookback, documentation of microbiologic culture or PCR, and receipt of a new antibiotic; (2) a sepsis enrichment step of structured chart review by trained non-physician study staff; and (3) discussion with the primary clinical team. Enrolled patients underwent physician adjudication into four diagnostic categories. To evaluate the enrichment step, we analyzed all patients screened during a 9-week period, assigned a composite "sepsis-likely" variable (CDC Adult Sepsis Event criteria or ICD-10 code R65.20/R65.21 within 48 hours before or after screening), and assessed mortality across each stage of screening. We also assessed concordance of the composite with physician adjudication among enrolled patients. ResultsFrom November 2023 through February 2026, 4,318 patients screened in through EHR-based automated screening; 1,220 (28%) were flagged for enrollment, and 288 were enrolled. Physician adjudication classified 209 (73%) as sepsis, 46 (16%) as infection without sepsis, 14 (5%) were classified as undifferentiated critical illness, and 19 (6.6%) as non-infectious sepsis mimics. Patients with sepsis were severely ill (median SOFA score, 9; ICU admission, 80%; shock, 48%), and 51% were immunocompromised; mortality was 14% in hospital and 27% at 90 days. In a 9-week sample of 907 screened encounters, 21% of those deferred and 70% of those flagged for enrollment met the sepsis-likely composite, a 3.3-fold increase in prevalence after structured study team review. ConclusionsA brief structured enrichment review after automated screening tripled the prevalence of EHR-based sepsis indicators among patients selected for enrollment, while concentrating enrollment efforts on roughly one-quarter of screened-in patients in this hospital-wide, all-source suspected-sepsis cohort. This approach may help prospective cohorts direct limited biospecimen resources toward patients most informative for host-response and biomarker research.

infographic.key_insight: A structured non-physician chart-review enrichment step after automated EHR screening helped narrow a very large sepsis candidate pool into a smaller, more clinically valid cohort for longitudinal research.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach may improve efficiency for sepsis studies by reducing false positives from broad SIRS-based screening while preserving patients most likely to have true sepsis.
method: Automated EHR screen: ≥2 SIRS criteria, microbiologic culture/PCR documentation, and a new antibiotic order.
Non-physician staff performed structured chart review as an enrichment step, then cases were discussed with the primary clinical team.
Enrolled patients were later physician-adjudicated into sepsis, infection without sepsis, undifferentiated critical illness, or non-infectious sepsis mimics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 4,318 screened patients, 1,220 were flagged and 288 enrolled; among enrolled patients, 73% were adjudicated as sepsis, and in a 9-week sample the enrichment step was associated with higher sepsis-likeness among those not deferred.
infographic.watch_item: Because this was a single-center workflow using a specific screening pipeline and a partial 9-week evaluation sample, generalizability and operational burden may differ at other hospitals.
infographic.paper_title: Efficiency of a Multi-step Screening and Enrichment Process for Prospective Sepsis Cohort Enrollment

title: A Zero-Shot Decision Model (Jev) Matches a Trained Classifier but Ranks Its Own Errors Worse: Calibrated, Split-Conformal Next-Procedure Recommendation in General Dentistry
authors: Rodrigues, C. C.; Rebello, S. D.
abstract: On real-world dental records, procedure history predicts the next procedure category well, and a simple history-aware classical model beats every large-language-model (LLM) design we tested. We study the question that follows every dental diagnosis: given a patients chart and most recent procedure, what should the dentist do next? Commercial dental artificial intelligence in 2026 is overwhelmingly diagnostic, and the closest published system for this sequencing task, MultiTP (Chen et al., 2024b), offers neither calibrated uncertainty, structured rationale, nor an evaluation as decision support. We introduce DentaCoPilot, a recommender that returns a calibrated top-K distribution over Current Dental Terminology (CDT) codes, a verbalised confidence label, an explicit abstain flag, and a chart-grounded rationale, and we compare four classical baselines with six LLM variants. On an apples-to-apples synthetic evaluation, classical baselines reach 0.567 top-1 while pure LLM variants trail at 0.267 to 0.467, and moving the backbone from Sonnet to Opus does not help. Prompt-conditioning a Sonnet LLM on the classical baselines candidate list closes most of the gap while preserving rationale and abstention; because the synthetic generator shares Markov structure with the bigram baseline, these synthetic rankings index pipeline behaviour, not externally valid clinical performance. We anchor external validity for the task on the public MEPS 2023 corpus (11,016 next-visit transitions across 5,088 patients): a history-aware model reaches 0.479 top-1 against 0.297 for a most-frequent baseline, is well calibrated (expected calibration error 0.031), and supports split-conformal selective prediction with a distribution-free coverage guarantee. A zero-shot LLM given only 1 this coarse history loses to the same classical baseline, so the LLMs value depends on rich charts rather than category history alone. Prospective clinician-in-the-loop validation and CDT-level real-data validation remain future work, contingent on clinical-data access and ethics approval that we have sought but not secured.

infographic.key_insight: A simple history-aware classical model outperformed all tested LLM variants for next dental procedure prediction, while the proposed DentaCoPilot added calibrated uncertainty, abstention, and chart-grounded rationale.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This work suggests decision support for dentistry may be more reliable when it combines prior procedure history with calibrated selective prediction rather than relying on zero-shot LLMs alone.
method: Compared 4 classical baselines and 6 LLM variants for next-procedure recommendation.
Built DentaCoPilot to output top-K CDT codes, confidence labels, an abstain flag, and a rationale.
Used split-conformal prediction to support selective prediction with coverage guarantees.
infographic.evidence_signal: On MEPS 2023 data (11,016 next-visit transitions from 5,088 patients), the history-aware model reached 0.479 top-1 accuracy versus 0.297 for a most-frequent baseline and had ECE 0.031; in synthetic tests, classical baselines reached 0.567 top-1 while pure LLMs ranged from 0.267 to 0.467.
infographic.watch_item: The synthetic evaluation reflects pipeline behavior rather than externally valid clinical performance, and CDT-level real-world validation plus clinician-in-the-loop testing are still needed.
infographic.paper_title: A Zero-Shot Decision Model (Jev) Matches a Trained Classifier but Ranks Its Own Errors Worse: Calibrated, Split-Conformal Next-Procedure Recommendation in General Dentistry

title: From examinations to consultations: a physician-reviewed Japanese benchmark for large language models in traditional Kampo medicine
authors: Takata, H.; Harada, Y.; Inoue, H.; Uneda, K.; Yoshino, T.; Nogami, T.
abstract: Objectives: Patients and clinicians increasingly ask large language models (LLMs) about Kampo, Japan's traditional medicine. Yet evaluations of LLMs have measured accuracy on examination questions, which ask what a model knows; a consultation asks whether it can apply that knowledge to the patient at hand. No benchmark had measured that. Materials and Methods: KampoBench comprises 74 consultation scenarios and 310 conversation-specific rubric criteria, following the design of HealthBench. Scenarios, criteria and reference answers were drafted by an LLM and revised by board-certified Kampo physicians. Ten current models from three vendors were evaluated. Because LLM graders are known to favor their own family, each response was graded by a model from each vendor. Results: The best model reached 74.8-86.3% across graders, the physician-revised reference answers 87.9-92.4%. Rankings were stable across graders (Spearman's rho 0.952-0.976), and the family-favoring deviation was 0.4 to 0.6 percentage points, below the bootstrap standard deviation of one measurement; grader leniency varied by 14.3 points. Models were most reliable on criteria about advising that care be sought (83.6%) and least reliable on those requiring a known crude-drug risk to be tied to the case (17.5%), though 79.2% of those responses named the drug. Discussion: The shortfall lay in applying knowledge to the case rather than in holding it - a distinction examination-format evaluations cannot make. Conclusion: Evaluation in traditional medicine should measure the judgments a consultation requires, not recall alone. Quoted alongside the grader that produced it, a KampoBench score is a usable measure of those judgments.

infographic.key_insight: KampoBench shifts LLM evaluation in Kampo medicine from recall-based exam questions to consultation-style judgment on patient-specific scenarios.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For clinical NLP, this benchmark better tests whether models can give context-aware traditional medicine guidance rather than only answer factual questions.
method: 74 physician-reviewed Kampo consultation scenarios
310 conversation-specific rubric criteria adapted from HealthBench
10 current models from 3 vendors; each answer graded by models from all three vendors plus physician-revised references
infographic.evidence_signal: The best model scored 74.8-86.3% across graders, while physician-revised reference answers scored 87.9-92.4%, with stable grader rankings (Spearman's rho 0.952-0.976).
infographic.watch_item: Grader leniency still varied by 14.3 points, so scores may depend on which grader is used even when family bias is small.
infographic.paper_title: From examinations to consultations: a physician-reviewed Japanese benchmark for large language models in traditional Kampo medicine

title: Machine Learning-Supported Efficient VTE Risk Assessment using Routinely Collected Electronic Health Record Data
authors: Li, Z.; Yagis, E.; Riad, A.; Windrath-Carr, O.; Arribas, M.; Sodiq, T.; Goldsmith, K.; Glampson, B.; Flott, K.; Haji, G.; Khan, Z.; Baker, C.; Mayer, E. K.
abstract: ObjectiveVenous thromboembolism (VTE) is a leading cause of preventable inpatient mortality, while the real-world performance of mandated risk assessment and the potential for automating using electronic health record (EHR) data remain unclear. We evaluated completion, concordance with structured EHR data, clinical validity, and feasibility of EHR-supported VTE risk assessment assisted by machine learning. Materials and MethodsWe analysed 577,904 admissions and 726,896 VTE assessment forms across five NHS hospitals between 2015 and 2025. Concordance and clinical validity were evaluated in 87,118 completed assessments from 2023 to 2024. Machine learning models compared clinician-recorded and EHR-derived risk factors in 74,372 encounters with an assessment completed within 14 hours of admission. ResultsOverall completion was 96.7%, and timely completion improved from 47.4% in 2015 to 90.5% in 2024. Agreement between forms and EHR data was good for common risk factors (e.g. age [≥] 60 years: precision 0.95, recall 0.77), but low-prevalence variables were often under-documented in the forms (e.g. critical care admission: precision 0.20, recall 0.14). Despite these discrepancies, form-derived thrombosis risk was associated with increased VTE incidence (adjusted OR 3.31, 95% CI 2.81-3.90). Models using EHR-derived factors available within 14 hours achieved an AUROC of 0.709, compared with 0.704 for clinician-recorded variables. DiscussionMuch of the information the risk assessment requires already exists in structured EHR data, and EHR-derived variables contained discriminative information comparable to that in clinician-recorded factors. ConclusionRoutinely collected EHR data could support real-time pre-population of structured VTE assessments, thereby reducing documentation burden while preserving clinical validity.

infographic.key_insight: Routinely collected EHR data can pre-populate VTE risk assessments with machine learning, matching clinician-recorded variables closely enough to support real-time documentation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could reduce clinician paperwork while preserving the clinical validity of inpatient VTE risk assessment workflows.
method: Analyzed 577,904 admissions and 726,896 VTE assessment forms across five NHS hospitals (2015–2025).
Compared form completion, timing, and concordance with structured EHR data in 87,118 assessments from 2023–2024.
Built ML models using EHR-derived versus clinician-recorded risk factors in 74,372 encounters completed within 14 hours of admission.
infographic.evidence_signal: Assessment completion was 96.7%, timely completion rose from 47.4% in 2015 to 90.5% in 2024, and EHR-derived models achieved AUROC 0.709 versus 0.704 for clinician-recorded variables.
infographic.watch_item: Some important low-prevalence risk factors were under-documented in forms, so automated pre-population still needs careful local validation and workflow integration.
infographic.paper_title: Machine Learning-Supported Efficient VTE Risk Assessment using Routinely Collected Electronic Health Record Data

title: Navigating Life After Dementia Diagnosis: Questions, Challenges, and Support Needs Among Dementia Dyads
authors: Britt, K.; Harb, A.; Bailey, B.; Saffold, B.; Luo, X.; Brown, R. T.; Huang, B.
abstract: BackgroundOlder adults living with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or Alzheimers disease and related dementias (AD/ADRD) and their care partners face substantial daily challenges that evolve with disease progression and extend far beyond the clinical setting, including symptom management, care coordination, healthcare navigation, and planning for future care needs. Understanding these challenges is essential for developing innovative solutions to provide ongoing and targeted support. In this study, we explored questions, challenges, and support needs dementia dyads experienced following diagnosis to inform the development of an artificial intelligence (AI)-based chatbot designed to provide ongoing support for dementia dyads. MethodsWe recruited 11 community-dwelling dyads comprising persons living with MCI or mild AD/ADRD and their care partners, one additional care partner, and 12 dementia care experts from academic medical centers, clinics, and aging organizations in the U.S. We conducted semi-structured interviews and analyzed them using conventional content analysis. ResultsParticipants described interconnected questions, challenges, and support needs that evolved while navigating life with MCI or AD/ADRD. Questions centered around day-to-day care management, medical concerns, behavioral symptom management, diagnosis and prognosis, safety, and resources and services. Challenges included care partner overwhelm, limited dementia knowledge, condition-related uncertainty, healthcare system navigation difficulties, financial constraints, and technology-related barriers. Participants identified needs for ongoing education, personalized care planning, resource navigation, logistical support and follow-up, culturally responsive care, and social and emotional support. ConclusionsDementia dyads experience substantial informational, emotional, and practical support needs in the early stages of MCI and AD/ADRD. Findings suggest that post-diagnostic support should extend beyond information provision alone to provide ongoing, personalized, and practical guidance that helps dyads navigate changing needs, resources, and everyday dementia care. These findings are informing the development of an AI-based chatbot intended to complement existing dementia care by extending access to education, practical guidance, and resource navigation between clinical encounters.

infographic.key_insight: After a dementia diagnosis, both people living with MCI/AD/ADRD and their care partners need ongoing, personalized help with daily care, navigation, and emotional support—not just one-time information.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Post-diagnostic support programs and AI tools may be more useful if they address practical care questions, care partner strain, and resource navigation over time.
method: 11 community-dwelling dementia dyads plus 1 additional care partner were interviewed
12 dementia care experts from academic medical centers, clinics, and aging organizations were also interviewed
Researchers used semi-structured interviews and conventional content analysis
infographic.evidence_signal: This was a qualitative interview study, so the evidence shows common needs and themes rather than testing whether an intervention improves outcomes.
infographic.watch_item: An AI chatbot may need careful design for cultural responsiveness, safety, privacy, and clear escalation pathways because needs are complex and change over time.
infographic.paper_title: Navigating Life After Dementia Diagnosis: Questions, Challenges, and Support Needs Among Dementia Dyads

title: Precision Evidence Bench: Assessing PICO alignment and faithful reporting in clinical AI
authors: Mukerji, A.; Sanghavi, N.; Lauritzen, T.; Muralidharan, J.; Gombar, S.
abstract: Clinicians routinely make decisions for patients whose comorbidities, prior therapies, laboratory abnormalities, or demographic characteristics are not reflected in the supporting evidence, even though these factors can influence treatment selection. Given this gap in the evidence base, we sought to evaluate how AI models respond to clinical questions in which patient characteristics or the treatment comparison and outcome of interest may affect the applicability of available evidence. We developed and publicly released Precision Evidence Bench, a benchmark of 209 synthetic clinical questions with specified population, intervention, comparator, and outcome (PICO) elements. Each answer is assessed using a five-item rubric that evaluates whether a single cited source matches the PICO and whether the answer faithfully reports its sources. The item verdicts determine one of five ratings, ranging from Precision match to Unsupported claim, without requiring a reference answer. We evaluated four frontier large language models (LLMs) using web search across all 209 questions, then repeated the evaluation with additional access to a corpus of precision evidence-based findings (pEBFs) designed to address these evidence gaps, using two corpus sizes. For every model, Precision match rates increased with the amount of precision evidence available, from 13 to 18% with web search alone to 17 to 28% with 100 million pEBFs and 41 to 56% with 500 million pEBFs. These findings suggest that access to matching evidence is an important determinant of LLM performance on precision medicine questions.

infographic.key_insight: LLMs answer precision-medicine questions more accurately when they can retrieve evidence that closely matches the patient’s PICO details.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For clinical decision support, having evidence that fits the patient scenario—not just any relevant paper—appears critical to producing faithful, usable AI responses.
method: Built Precision Evidence Bench: 209 synthetic clinical questions with explicit PICO elements.
Scored answers with a five-item rubric for PICO match and faithful source reporting.
Tested four frontier LLMs with web search, then with added precision evidence corpora of 100M and 500M pEBFs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Precision match rates rose from 13–18% with web search alone to 17–28% with 100M pEBFs and 41–56% with 500M pEBFs across models.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from synthetic questions and retrieval settings, so real-world clinical use still needs careful validation for safety, coverage, and citation faithfulness.
infographic.paper_title: Precision Evidence Bench: Assessing PICO alignment and faithful reporting in clinical AI

title: Multi-centre validation of MELD-graph for automated focal cortical dysplasia detection using 7T compared to paired 3T MRI
authors: Kronlage, C.; Ripart, M.; Piper, R. J.; Casella, C.; Klodowski, K.; Bauer, T.; Eriksson, M. H.; Bridgen, P.; Tisdall, M. M.; Bouschery, S. R.; Lange, A.; Pracht, E. D.; Stocker, T.; Cleary, J. O.; D'Arco, F.; Baldeweg, T.; Duncan, J. S.; Surges, R.; Ruber, T.; Rodgers, C. T.; Cope, T. E.; Carmichael, D. W.; O'Muircheartaigh, J.; Adler, S.; Wagstyl, K.
abstract: BackgroundSoftware tools can support MRI diagnosis of focal cortical dysplasias (FCDs) - subtle, surgically-treatable lesions that underlie drug-resistant focal epilepsy (DRFE). MELD-graph, a widely used open-source tool combining surface-based morphometry with a convolutional neural network, was developed using 1.5T and 3T MRI data. 7T MRI is increasingly used for lesion detection in DRFE. This study investigated whether MELD-graph is robust to domain shift at 7T. MethodsWe collated paired 3T and 7T T1-weighted MRI, and FLAIR where available, from 23 patients with FCD (6 histologically-verified, 17 identified radiologically) and 39 healthy controls at four epilepsy centres. Manual lesion labels were used as ground truth. MELD-graph was run on 3T images, on 7T images with the default pipeline, and on 7T images with adaptations for 7T MRI (SPM bias-field correction, SynthStrip skull-stripping, sub-millimetric FreeSurfer reconstruction), with and without ComBat harmonisation. FCD detection performance and surface morphometry features were compared. ResultsSensitivity for FCD detection was 65% (15/23) at 3T, 48% (11/23) for 7T default and 52% (12/23) for 7T adapted, with Combat harmonisation. Among radiologically 3T-negative patients, 2/8 were detected at 3T and 3/8 at 7T; and among histologically confirmed FCD, 3/6 at 3T and 1/6 at 7T. Specificity was significantly lower at 7T (default 39%, adapted 45%) than 3T (76%). False-positives predominantly occurred in the basal temporal lobes. ComBat harmonisation improved specificity in all conditions and largely compensated for field-strength dependent differences in surface morphometry features. Adding FLAIR at 7T increased false-positive predictions. ConclusionSensitivity is comparable but specificity of MELD-graph is lower at 7T compared to 3T. Adaptations for 7T MRI can reduce segmentation errors but do not significantly improve FCD detection, while harmonisation improves performance. The adapted pipeline is released open-source. 7T MELD-graph outputs may inform radiologist review in challenging cases but require cautious interpretation.

infographic.key_insight: MELD-graph detected focal cortical dysplasia at 7T with similar sensitivity to 3T, but specificity was notably worse unless harmonisation was used.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For epilepsy imaging workflows, 7T MELD-graph may help flag difficult lesions for review, but its higher false-positive rate means results should be interpreted cautiously.
method: Paired 3T and 7T MRI from 23 FCD patients and 39 healthy controls across four epilepsy centres.
Compared MELD-graph on 3T, on 7T default settings, and on 7T with adaptations for bias correction, skull-stripping, and sub-millimetric reconstruction.
Tested the effect of ComBat harmonisation and assessed surface morphometry plus lesion detection performance.
infographic.evidence_signal: In this multi-centre evaluation, sensitivity was 65% at 3T versus 48-52% at 7T, while specificity dropped from 76% at 3T to 39-45% at 7T and improved with ComBat harmonisation.
infographic.watch_item: 7T outputs produced more false positives, especially in the basal temporal lobes, so the pipeline should not be used as a stand-alone decision tool.
infographic.paper_title: Multi-centre validation of MELD-graph for automated focal cortical dysplasia detection using 7T compared to paired 3T MRI

title: Prospective validation of an uncertainty-aware machine learning model for secondary progressive multiple sclerosis classification
authors: Parakkal Sreenivasan, A.; Noui, Y.; Erngren, I.; Spjuth, O.; Burman, J.; Kultima, K.
abstract: Background: Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) often progresses to secondary-progressive MS (SPMS), but diagnosis is typically retrospective, delaying potential interventions. Existing rule-based and machine learning approaches often lack prospective validation and provide no uncertainty estimates, limiting clinical adoption. Objective: To prospectively evaluate a conformal prediction (CP)-enabled random forest model for reproducing clinician-recorded disease course labels in the Swedish Multiple Sclerosis Registry (SMSReg) and compare its classifications with the Lorscheider criteria. Methods: The CP model was trained and calibrated on SMSReg-2022 (10,787 individuals, 85,461 hospital visits) and then validated on SMSReg-2025 (15,719 individuals, 45,077 hospital visits; not included in the SMSReg-2022 training/calibration/testing datasets). Performance was assessed at the hospital visit and individual levels and compared with the Lorscheider criteria. Results: The model maintained good calibration on the prospective dataset. At the per-hospital visit-level, the model accuracies were 92% (RRMS) and 95% (SPMS). At the individual level, sensitivity was 98%, specificity 89%, and F1-score 0.75. With clinician-recorded labels as reference, the model showed higher sensitivity than the Lorscheider criteria (98% vs. 71%), more transition assignments (90% vs. 57%), and higher F1-score (0.76 vs. 0.69). Conclusion: The CP-enabled model prospectively reproduced clinician-recorded disease course labels with calibrated uncertainty, supporting harmonization and decision support.

infographic.key_insight: A conformal prediction–enabled random forest prospectively classified multiple sclerosis disease course with calibrated uncertainty, closely matching clinician-recorded labels.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could help standardize secondary progressive MS identification and support earlier, more consistent decision-making in registry and clinical workflows.
method: Trained and calibrated on Swedish MS Registry 2022 data.
Prospectively validated on an independent 2025 registry cohort not used in training.
Compared performance against clinician labels and Lorscheider criteria.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using 10,787 people for training/calibration and 15,719 for prospective validation, the model achieved 92% RRMS and 95% SPMS visit-level accuracy, with 98% sensitivity and 89% specificity at the individual level.
infographic.watch_item: Although promising, performance was evaluated against registry clinician-recorded labels and may require further external validation before broader clinical implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Prospective validation of an uncertainty-aware machine learning model for secondary progressive multiple sclerosis classification

title: Mapping polygenic risk scores to brain cells: insights for neurodegenerative diseases
authors: Simmonds, E.; McKeever, A.; Yaman, U.; Leonenko, G.; Kimatova, K.; Taylor, P.; Chandran, S.; Ryten, M.; Khakh, B.; O'Brien, J. T.; Spires-Jones, T.; Salih, D. A.; Escott-Price, V.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs) are driven by multiple related yet distinct pathological processes that evolve over decades, resulting in substantial clinical and neuropathological heterogeneity. Postmortem examinations of older individuals frequently reveal multiple coexisting neuropathologies, however, the underlying pathological processes cannot be easily assessed directly in living individuals. To quantify pathology-specific genetic signatures, we analysed a spectrum of NDDs using polygenic risk scores (PRSs) in the UK Biobank, restricting analyses to genes reported to be expressed in major brain cell-types, including microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and neurons. We found substantial overlap among purportedly cell-type specific gene sets (21-29%), with APOE or neighbouring genes from the APOE locus represented in all gene sets, indicating that current cell-type specific annotations capture considerable shared genetic variation across cell-types. Jointly, cell-type specific PRSs explained a large proportion (60-93%) of the genetic liability for NDDs in which dementia is a major clinical manifestation. Alzheimers disease (AD) showed associations across all cell-types, with oligodendrocyte- and astrocyte-based PRSs demonstrating strong effects independent of APOE. AD PRS and APOE status independently differentiated Parkinsons disease (PD) with dementia from PD without dementia. PD without dementia and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) exhibited distinct genetic profiles, with limited overlap with other NDDs. Collectively, these findings reveal both shared and disease-specific genetic contributions across neurodegenerative disorders and demonstrate that currently available cell-type specific gene sets capture substantial overlapping genetic risk. The imperfect alignment between clinical phenotypes and underlying pathology, coupled with the extensive overlap of gene expression across these cell types, underscores the persistent challenges in resolving the genetic architecture of neurodegenerative diseases and elucidating their underlying biological mechanisms.

infographic.key_insight: Cell-type-focused polygenic risk scores reveal that neurodegenerative disease genetics are partly shared across brain cell types, but also retain disease-specific patterns, especially for Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease with dementia, Parkinson’s without dementia, and ALS.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These findings may help researchers better stratify neurodegenerative risk and distinguish overlapping dementia-related biology, but they are not yet ready for direct clinical use.
method: Analyzed polygenic risk scores in UK Biobank across multiple neurodegenerative diseases.
Restricted genetic analyses to genes reported in major brain cell types: microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and neurons.
Compared cell-type-specific scores and APOE-related effects across disease phenotypes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports substantial overlap among cell-type gene sets (21-29%) and that combined cell-type PRSs explained 60-93% of genetic liability for NDDs with major dementia involvement.
infographic.watch_item: Current cell-type gene annotations overlap heavily, so these PRS signals may reflect shared genetics rather than cleanly separated cell-specific biology.
infographic.paper_title: Mapping polygenic risk scores to brain cells: insights for neurodegenerative diseases

title: Data-efficient machine learning for the detection of duodenal neoplasia: a multi-centre study
authors: Di Lisio, F.; Soilleux, E. J.; Jaeckle, F.
abstract: BackgroundMachine Learning (ML) has shown promise in histopathological diagnosis, but rare tumours, like duodenal epithelial neoplasms, are challenging because large, labelled datasets are difficult to assemble. We propose a data-efficient ML pipeline for detecting duodenal epithelial neoplasia in whole-slide images. MethodsWe assembled a five-hospital dataset of haematoxylin and eosin-stained duodenal biopsy whole slide images (WSIs) at 10x magnification, comprising 8,027 normal and 401 neoplastic biopsies, including adenomas, carcinomas and neuroendocrine tumours. WSIs were divided into patches and encoded using the Hibou-B foundation model. We compared global standardisation with unsupervised site-specific standardisation of patch embeddings. Our pipeline combined principal component analysis, a Gaussian mixture model and a Random Forest classifier. We assessed generalisability using leave-one-hospital-out cross-validation across four hospitals and on an independent test set from a fifth hospital. ResultsIn leave-one-hospital-out cross-validation, the pipeline achieved a mean accuracy of 90%, sensitivity of 96%, specificity of 83% and an AUC of 0.96. On the external test hospital, it achieved 94% accuracy, 93% sensitivity, 95% specificity, and AUC of 0.97. Site-specific standardisation improved mean cross-validation accuracy by 20 percentage points compared with global standardisation, while the Gaussian mixture pipeline improved accuracy by 12 percentage points compared with mean pooling of patch embeddings. ConclusionsWe present a data-efficient ML approach for detecting duodenal epithelial neoplasia from WSIs. Strong performance was maintained across hospitals and on an independent external test cohort despite the limited number of neoplastic training cases, supporting the feasibility of foundation-model-based approaches for rare histopathological diagnoses.

infographic.key_insight: A foundation-model-based, data-efficient pipeline can detect duodenal epithelial neoplasia on whole-slide biopsy images with strong accuracy across hospitals.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could help pathology teams screen rare duodenal lesions more consistently, even when local labelled data are limited.
method: H&E-stained duodenal biopsy WSIs from 5 hospitals were split into patches and encoded with the Hibou-B foundation model.
Patch embeddings were standardized using either global or site-specific unsupervised normalization, then reduced with PCA.
A Gaussian mixture model and Random Forest classifier were evaluated with leave-one-hospital-out cross-validation and an external test hospital.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study used 8,027 normal and 401 neoplastic biopsies; performance reached 90% mean accuracy in cross-validation and 94% accuracy on an independent external hospital set.
infographic.watch_item: Results are promising, but real-world deployment will still need prospective validation and careful checks for site-specific workflow differences.
infographic.paper_title: Data-efficient machine learning for the detection of duodenal neoplasia: a multi-centre study

title: Full stack academic publishing in seizures with artificial intelligence: a cautionary tale
authors: Kerr, W. T.; Pellinen, J.; McFarlane, K. N.; Goldenholz, D. M.
abstract: SignificanceThere is potential for generative artificial intelligence (AI) to perform "full stack" academic publishing, including comprehensive manuscript fabrication, "peer"-review, and editorial decision making. This study evaluated the benefits and cautions in using AI for full stack academic publishing in clinical research about seizures. MethodsThree epileptologists each selected 1 published manuscript in Epilepsia and produced an AI-fabricated manuscript about seizures. AI tools were then used to perform "peer"-review and make editorial decisions with minimal human supervision. The rates of identifying AI-fabricated manuscripts and editorial decisions among the epileptologists was analyzed, and epileptologists observations on how AI differed from typical human "peer"-review and editorial decisions was collected. ResultsFour of 6 (67%) pairs of AI-fabricated and human-generated manuscripts were correctly identified. Only 1 AI-fabricated manuscript was editorially rejected, whereas another had a subtle indicator of fabrication. When compared to human content, AI generated content was comprehensive, detailed, and based on the highest standard of academic publication. However, generated content was more verbose, used more structured responses, and more critical feedback. ConclusionsThese results demonstrate that the quality of AI-fabricated manuscripts about clinical research in seizures was sufficiently high that the current methods of peer and editorial review could not easily distinguish fabricated content compared to human-written content. Moreover, AI review and editorial decisions were high quality and appeared reasonable in many cases. AI tools have matured to the point that there should be thoughtful policies that permit AI assistance but prohibit insufficiently supervised autonomous scientific submissions, reviews, and editorial decisions. Highlights- The maturity of AI tools to assist in manuscript generation, peer-review, and editorial decisions comes with cautions. - Only 1 of 3 artificial intelligence (AI) fabricated manuscripts about seizures were reliably identified and rejected. - This study describes characteristics of AI-generated peer-review and editorial comments that had insufficient human oversight.

infographic.key_insight: AI can produce seizure-related manuscripts, peer reviews, and editorial decisions that look convincingly human, raising important concerns about unsupervised scientific publishing.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For clinical researchers and editors, the key takeaway is that AI assistance may be useful, but fully autonomous AI-driven manuscript submission or review could undermine trust in the publication process.
method: Three epileptologists each chose one published Epilepsia article.
They used AI to fabricate seizure-related manuscripts and to generate peer reviews and editorial decisions.
Human experts then tried to identify AI-fabricated papers and judge the editorial outcomes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experts correctly identified 4 of 6 AI-fabricated vs human-generated manuscript pairs, and only 1 of 3 AI-fabricated manuscripts was clearly rejected by editorial decision.
infographic.watch_item: A major concern is that current peer review may not reliably distinguish high-quality AI-generated content from authentic human-authored research, especially without strong human oversight.
infographic.paper_title: Full stack academic publishing in seizures with artificial intelligence: a cautionary tale

title: A Multi-Domain EEG Framework Integrating Spectral, Functional Connectivity, and Topological Features for Subject-Level ADHD Classification
authors: Rohani, F.; Mostafavi, S.; Ebrahimifakhar, P.; Zomorrodi, R.; Mueller, A.
abstract: BackgroundAttention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that significantly affect cognitive, academic, and social functioning. Although electroencephalography (EEG) has emerged as a promising non-invasive tool for identifying objective neurophysiological biomarkers of ADHD because of its high temporal resolution and cost-effectiveness, many existing machine learning studies rely on single-domain EEG features, which may not adequately capture the complex functional organization of the brain. MethodsThis study proposes a subject-level EEG classification framework that integrates three complementary feature domains: spectral characteristics, weighted Phase Lag Index (wPLI)-based functional connectivity, and topological descriptors derived from persistent homology. EEG recordings from 121 subjects were preprocessed and segmented into overlapping windows for feature extraction. Window-level features were aggregated to generate subject-level representations. Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) was employed to select the 110 most informative features from an initial set of 1,043 descriptors. Five machine learning classifiers, including Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), were evaluated using stratified five-fold cross-validation. An ablation study was further conducted to assess the contribution of each feature domain. Model interpretability was investigated using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), two widely adopted Explainable Artificial Intelligence techniques for interpreting machine learning models. ResultsAmong the evaluated classifiers, the SVM achieved the highest classification performance, yielding an accuracy of 80.17%, an F1-score of 80.95%, a balanced accuracy of 80.14%, a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 86.72%, and a precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) of 87.34%. The ablation study demonstrated that combining spectral, functional connectivity, and topological features consistently outperformed individual feature domains, highlighting the complementary nature of these representations. Explainable AI analyses further identified functional connectivity features as the primary contributors to classification performance while confirming the additional value of spectral and topological descriptors. ConclusionsThe proposed framework demonstrates that integrating spectral analysis, functional connectivity, and topological data analysis provides an effective and interpretable approach for subject-level ADHD classification from EEG recordings. The combination of recursive feature selection, multi-domain feature fusion, ablation analysis, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence establishes a transparent and reproducible pipeline that may facilitate the development of reliable EEG-based clinical decision-support systems for ADHD.

infographic.key_insight: A multi-domain EEG model combining spectral, connectivity, and topological features improved subject-level ADHD classification, with SVM performing best.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This suggests EEG-based machine learning may help support more objective ADHD biomarker research, though it is not ready to replace clinical assessment.
method: EEG from 121 subjects was preprocessed and split into overlapping windows for feature extraction.
Three feature domains were combined: spectral features, wPLI functional connectivity, and persistent homology topological descriptors.
RFE selected 110 features from 1,043 total descriptors; five classifiers were tested with stratified five-fold cross-validation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The best model, an SVM, achieved 80.17% accuracy, 80.95% F1-score, 80.14% balanced accuracy, 86.72% ROC-AUC, and 87.34% PR-AUC.
infographic.watch_item: Performance comes from a relatively small sample and cross-validation on a single dataset, so external validation is needed before broader use.
infographic.paper_title: A Multi-Domain EEG Framework Integrating Spectral, Functional Connectivity, and Topological Features for Subject-Level ADHD Classification

title: A spatial AI-based biomarker with independent prognostic value in early low- and intermediate- risk breast cancer
authors: Boissin, C.; Xiang, Y.; Liu, B.; Vallon-Christersson, J.; Walker, E.; Hartman, J.; Rantalainen, M.
abstract: BackgroundPatients with ER-positive/HER2-negative early breast cancer of low or intermediate grade are generally considered to have a favourable prognosis, yet a number will recur. This risk is poorly captured by standard clinicopathological factors. AI-based medical devices for whole slide image (WSI) analyses used for risk-stratification often predict on slide-level thereby overlooking spatial localisation of the biomarkers. We hypothesise that the spatial distribution of a previously reported AI-based marker provides independent prognostic value beyond its global score. Patients and MethodsThis Swedish multicentre cohort study includes 6106 patients with primary invasive breast cancer: 3078 from the Stockholm region (training) and 3028 from Sk[a]ne (independent test). Tile-level high-grade morphology scores were generated with ViT_DG, a vision-transformer adaptation of DeepGrade, and the presence of clusters of high-risk tiles localised at the invasive tumour front was defined as a binary biomarker. Primary analyses were pre-specified in the ER-positive/HER2-negative/lymph-node-negative and Grade 1-2 subgroup. Association with breast-cancer recurrence-free interval (BCRFI) and distant metastasis were assessed using multivariable Cox proportional hazards models (HR). ResultsIn the primary subgroup (n=1536 training; n=1403 test), tumour front clusters were present in 37% and 39% of patients. Cluster-positive status was associated with a 2.30-fold increased risk in the external test. Cluster-negative patients achieved a 10-year BCRFI of 95.3%, equivalent to Grade 1 patients and better than Grade 2 (92.4%), whereas cluster-positive patients (90.2%) did worse than the Grade 3 reference. The association was retained in patients classified as low-risk by ViT_DG (test set multivariable HR 2.86), identifying high-risk patients not captured by the global score. ConclusionsThe absence of high-risk morphology clusters at the tumour front is an independent prognostic indicator, identifying a low-risk group independently of the global AI biomarker classification. More broadly, preserving the spatial distribution of AI-derived predictions enables prognostic stratification beyond slide-level aggregation. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT02306096

infographic.key_insight: In early ER-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer, the absence of high-risk morphology clusters at the tumour front identifies a lower-risk group beyond the paper’s global AI score.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Spatially localizing AI predictions on whole-slide images may improve prognostic stratification and help flag patients whose recurrence risk is underestimated by standard clinicopathologic factors or slide-level scoring alone.
method: Swedish multicentre cohort of 6,106 primary invasive breast cancer patients; 3,078 training and 3,028 independent external test.
Used tile-level high-grade morphology scores from a vision-transformer model (ViT_DG/DeepGrade adaptation).
Defined a binary biomarker based on clusters of high-risk tiles at the invasive tumour front and tested associations with recurrence outcomes using multivariable Cox models.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the pre-specified ER-positive/HER2-negative/lymph-node-negative/Grade 1–2 subgroup, tumour-front clusters were seen in 37% of training and 39% of test patients and were linked to about a 2.30-fold higher recurrence risk in the external test set.
infographic.watch_item: This biomarker is derived from a specific retrospective multicentre dataset and needs prospective validation and robust slide-scanning/segmentation standardization before routine use.
infographic.paper_title: A spatial AI-based biomarker with independent prognostic value in early low- and intermediate- risk breast cancer

title: Microbial traits have minimal power for predicting death from bloodstream infection
authors: Gilliland, R.; Valdes-Tresanco, M. E.; Plakhotnyk, A.; Westlund, A.; Smith, J. T.; Pham, T. M.; Mortimer, T. D.; Walker, B. J.; Earl, A. M.; Grad, Y. H.; MacDonald, M. E.; Lewis, I. A.; PRIME Consortium,
abstract: Bloodstream infection (BSI) is a life-threatening condition where the risk of dying is affected by both patient-and pathogen-related factors. Certain microbial traits (e.g., virulence genes) are thought to affect survival rates from BSIs, but the magnitude of their impact on human mortality remains unclear. To address this, we analyzed the microbial genomes, quantitative proteomes, and electronic medical records (EMRs) from 35,746 BSIs from Calgary, Canada (2006-2022). We show that EMR-based machine learning models accurately predict 30-day mortality (AUC=0.83), but surprisingly, integrating >70,000 microbial genes/proteins does not improve this performance. We demonstrate that microbial factors co-segregate with specific patient cohorts and are therefore not independent predictors of risk. We conclude that microbial virulence factors have minimal impact on mortality rates from BSIs. One-Sentence SummaryMicrobial genes and protein abundance levels have minimal power for predicting 30-day mortality in bloodstream infections.

infographic.key_insight: Patient clinical data predicted 30-day bloodstream-infection mortality well, while adding microbial genes and proteins provided little to no extra predictive value.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For risk stratification in bloodstream infection, the biggest gains likely come from patient-level EMR models rather than pathogen trait profiling alone.
method: Analyzed 35,746 bloodstream infections from Calgary (2006–2022).
Combined electronic medical records with microbial genomes and quantitative proteomes (>70,000 microbial features).
Compared mortality prediction performance with and without microbial features using machine-learning models.
infographic.evidence_signal: EMR-based models predicted 30-day mortality with AUC=0.83, and adding microbial genes/proteins did not improve performance.
infographic.watch_item: The findings suggest microbial traits may be cohort-linked rather than independently predictive, so results may not generalize equally across settings or populations.
infographic.paper_title: Microbial traits have minimal power for predicting death from bloodstream infection

title: COMBINING CHEST X-RAY AND CLINICAL COVARIATES FOR OSTEOPOROSIS SCREENING: A MULTIMODAL DEEP LEARNING APPROACH
authors: kobayashi, v.; Baluyut, G.; Punsalan, J.
abstract: Osteoporosis is a major global health concern, yet screening remains inaccessible in many economically challenged and low-resource settings due to the high cost and operational complexity the gold standard Dual-energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DXA) scan requires. This study presents a multimodal deep-learning approach for opportunistic osteoporosis screening using chest X-rays and clinical variables such as age and gender. A total of 406 samples were retrospectively collected from a national hospital, comprising annotated chest radiographs paired with their DXA results from patients 50 and above. Two convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, ResNet50 and EfficientNetb3, were deployed under three configurations: image-only, early fusion, and late fusion. Image preprocessing includes CLAHE+Gamma Correction, followed by resizing, local regions of interest (ROI) extraction, and augmentation. The multimodal integration was conducted via early fusion (pixel-level) and late fusion (feature-level), with clinical variables normalized and encoded into a 1x3 vector. A custom Residual MLP classifier was employed in the late fusion models. Hyperparameter tuning was performed using Optunas Bayesian optimization. Evaluation metrics included Accuracy, AUC, Precision, Recall, Sensitivity, and F1 Score. Among all models, Late Fusion EfficientNetb3 achieved the best performance on the global chest X-ray, with an AUC of 72.73%. Moreover, EfficientNetb3 consistently outperformed the ResNet50 architecture across all local ROI, Right Clavicle, Right Scapula, and Spine, with fusion models yielding higher sensitivity and balanced classification. The framework achieved competitive diagnostic performance despite the limitations of chest radiographs and an imbalanced dataset. Moreover, the findings demonstrated the feasibility of integrating chest X-rays with clinical covariates for AI-assisted osteoporosis screening, aiming to fill the accessibility gaps in preventive bone health diagnostics.

infographic.key_insight: Combining chest X-rays with basic clinical variables improved AI-based osteoporosis screening, with late-fusion EfficientNetB3 performing best overall.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could help identify patients at higher osteoporosis risk using existing chest radiographs when DXA access is limited.
method: Retrospective study of 406 patients aged 50+ with chest X-rays linked to DXA results.
Compared ResNet50 and EfficientNetB3 in image-only, early-fusion, and late-fusion settings.
Used CLAHE + gamma correction, ROI extraction, augmentation, and Optuna-tuned models with a residual MLP for late fusion.
infographic.evidence_signal: Late-Fusion EfficientNetB3 achieved the top global chest X-ray result, with AUC 72.73%, and performed consistently better than ResNet50 across local ROI analyses.
infographic.watch_item: The dataset was small and imbalanced, so performance may not generalize without external validation and prospective testing.
infographic.paper_title: COMBINING CHEST X-RAY AND CLINICAL COVARIATES FOR OSTEOPOROSIS SCREENING: A MULTIMODAL DEEP LEARNING APPROACH

title: AI-Assisted Tissue-Based Antibody Interpretation in Autoimmune Encephalitis: Prospective Validation and Reader Study
authors: Cao, Z.; Xie, D.; Zou, S.; Li, D.; Martinez-Martinez, P.; Zong, S.; Zhang, Z.
abstract: Tissue-based assays provide broad screening for neural autoantibodies but remain vulnerable to technical and reader-dependent variability. We evaluated an integrated workflow combining automated 3,3'-diaminobenzidine tissue-based assay processing, digital whole-slide imaging, and interpretable deep learning. Model development used 2,357 retrospective serum and cerebrospinal fluid images referred from more than 80 institutions and processed in a centralized laboratory, with reference labels established by expert-consensus tissue-based assay interpretation. A prospective validation cohort included 200 images from 200 unique patients (154 positive and 46 negative; 100 serum and 100 cerebrospinal fluid). The same images were evaluated by two expert and two novice readers in a fixed-order two-round study, with unaided interpretation followed by artificial-intelligence-assisted interpretation after a washout of at least two weeks. The standalone binary classifier achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.922, accuracy of 86.5%, sensitivity of 85.7%, and specificity of 89.1% in prospective validation. Pooled reader accuracy was 90.4% in the unaided round and 97.4% in the artificial-intelligence-assisted round (McNemar P < 0.001), with specificity of 82.6% and 99.5%, respectively. Novice-reader accuracy was 83.3% unaided and 96.5% with artificial-intelligence assistance (P < 0.001), approaching unaided expert accuracy of 97.5%. Among tissue-based-assay-positive cases, reader accuracy for cytoplasmic/nuclear antigen-associated versus neural surface antigen-associated staining-pattern subclassification was 88.8% unaided and 94.0% with artificial-intelligence assistance (P < 0.001). These findings support further multicentre, cross-platform evaluation of artificial-intelligence-assisted neural autoantibody tissue interpretation. Abbreviated summaryCao et al. report prospective validation of an automated tissue-based neural autoantibody workflow combining digital imaging and interpretable deep learning. Artificial-intelligence-assisted reading was associated with higher interpretation accuracy, particularly among less-experienced readers, supporting further multicentre validation across laboratories and imaging platforms.

infographic.key_insight: An AI-assisted workflow for tissue-based neural autoantibody interpretation improved reader accuracy, especially for novice readers, and outperformed unaided interpretation in a prospective validation study.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could help standardize autoimmune encephalitis antibody screening and reduce reader-dependent variability in pathology-style tissue interpretation.
method: Trained on 2,357 retrospective serum and CSF tissue-based assay images from >80 institutions
Prospectively tested on 200 new images from 200 patients using a binary classifier
Compared 2 expert and 2 novice readers in unaided vs AI-assisted rounds after a washout period
infographic.evidence_signal: In prospective validation, the standalone classifier achieved AUC 0.922, and AI assistance increased pooled reader accuracy from 90.4% to 97.4% with specificity rising from 82.6% to 99.5%.
infographic.watch_item: Results came from a centralized workflow and fixed-order reader study, so multicenter cross-platform validation is still needed before broad deployment.
infographic.paper_title: AI-Assisted Tissue-Based Antibody Interpretation in Autoimmune Encephalitis: Prospective Validation and Reader Study

title: Clinical utility of plasma APOE proteotyping for Alzheimer's disease risk and prognosis
authors: Shi, R.; Choity, L. T.; Farinas, M. F.; Zeng, X.; Emanuel, J. E.; Saeed, A.; Reis, S. E.; Lopez, O. L.; Kamboh, M. I.; Cohen, A. D.; Gildengers, A. G.; Wilckens, K. A.; Karikari, T. K.
abstract: BackgroundAlzheimers disease (AD) is a complex neurodegenerative disorder strongly influenced by genetic factors, with apolipoprotein E (APOE) {varepsilon}4 allele being the most established risk variant. Although DNA-based genotyping remains standard, plasma proteotyping may provide scalable, isoform-specific alternatives. Here, we aimed to investigate the clinical utility of APOE proteotyping as a surrogate for genotyping in different clinical and research cohorts. MethodsPlasma APOE4 protein were quantified using the NULISAseq CNS panel across four cohorts (ADRC, HeartSCORE, LATTICE, and ALPS). DNA-based APOE genotyping was the reference standard. Proteotyping thresholds for APOE {varepsilon}4 carrier status and copy number were derived in ADRC and externally validated in the other cohorts. Logistic, proportional-odds, and Cox proportional-hazards models compared genotype- and proteotype-defined groups in relation to amyloid positivity, cross-sectional CDR global scores, and time to CDR-SB worsening, respectively. ResultsPlasma APOE4 accurately classified APOE {varepsilon}4 carrier status in ADRC (AUC=0.977, 95%CI 0.967-0.985; threshold 5.78 NULISA protein quantification [NPQ] value) and achieved near-perfect external validation in HeartSCORE, LATTICE, and ALPS (all AUCs=1.000, 95%CI 1.000-1.000). Plasma APOE4 also well-differentiated heterozygous from homozygous {varepsilon}4 carriers (ADRC AUC=0.879, 95%CI 0.834-0.921; threshold 12.23 NPQ value). Genotype- and proteotype-defined {varepsilon}4 carrier status showed similar associations with amyloid positivity (OR=4.40 vs 4.45), higher CDR global scores (OR=1.50 for both), and CDR-SB worsening (HR=1.22 for both). DiscussionPlasma APOE4 proteotyping accurately distinguished genotype-defined APOE {varepsilon}4 carrier status and copy number while demonstrating AD-related associations comparable to DNA genotyping.

infographic.key_insight: Plasma APOE4 proteotyping can closely mirror DNA-based APOE ε4 genotyping for identifying carrier status and even distinguishing heterozygous from homozygous carriers.
infographic.clinical_relevance: If validated broadly, this blood-based assay could offer a scalable alternative for APOE-related risk stratification and research enrollment in Alzheimer’s disease.
method: Measured plasma APOE4 with the NULISAseq CNS panel in four cohorts.
Used ADRC to set thresholds for ε4 carrier status and copy number.
Validated performance against DNA genotyping and compared associations with amyloid positivity, CDR scores, and CDR-SB worsening.
infographic.evidence_signal: Performance was very strong: AUC 0.977 in ADRC and 1.000 in three external cohorts for ε4 carrier detection, with similar AD-related associations to genotype-based analyses.
infographic.watch_item: The findings are promising but need broader real-world validation before plasma proteotyping can replace genotyping in routine clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: Clinical utility of plasma APOE proteotyping for Alzheimer's disease risk and prognosis

title: Can Routine Clinical Variables Substitute for Urine Albumin Testing in Moderate Chronic Kidney Disease? A Machine Learning Analysis of NHANES 2015 to 2018
authors: SAXENA, J. N.; Potturu, D. V. P.; Nagraj, A.
abstract: BackgroundAlbuminuria is central to staging and risk prediction in chronic kidney disease (CKD), yet urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) testing is performed far less often than serum creatinine testing. Whether routinely available clinical variables can identify patients likely to have albuminuria, and so substitute for or prioritize testing, is unclear. MethodsWe analyzed adults in NHANES 2015-2018 with an eGFR of 30-59 mL/min/1.73m2 (CKD-EPI 2021). The outcome was UACR[≥] 30 mg/g. Seventeen features derived from demographics, serum creatinine, eGFR, blood pressure, diabetes status and self-reported kidney disease were used; UACR was excluded. Logistic regression, random forest and gradient boosting were evaluated with 10-times repeated stratified 5-fold cross-validation. We report AUC with bootstrap 95% CIs, DeLong tests, calibration, survey-weighted AUC, diabetes subgroups and a rule-out analysis. ResultsOf 687 participants, 239 (34.8%) had UACR[≥] 30 mg/g. Discrimination was modest and similar across models: logistic regression AUC 0.723 (95% CI 0.684-0.762), random forest 0.721 (0.680-0.761; DeLong p = 0.84 vs logistic regression) and gradient boosting 0.719 (0.679-0.759; p = 0.76). Logistic regression and random forest were reasonably calibrated (slopes 0.87 and 0.98); gradient boosting was overfitted (slope 0.64). Discrimination was lower in participants without diabetes (logistic regression AUC 0.636 vs 0.722 with diabetes). Using logistic regression to rule out testing at 90% sensitivity would have spared 22.7% of participants from testing but missed 23 of 239 cases; at 95% sensitivity, only 16.3% would have been spared. ConclusionsRoutine clinical variables identify albuminuria only modestly, and flexible machine-learning models offer no advantage over logistic regression. No model allowed a meaningful share of patients to forgo UACR testing without missing cases, supporting universal UACR testing in moderate CKD.

infographic.key_insight: Routine clinical variables could only modestly predict albuminuria in moderate CKD, and machine-learning models did not outperform logistic regression.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These findings support continuing universal UACR testing rather than trying to replace it with prediction based on standard clinical data.
method: NHANES 2015–2018 adults with eGFR 30–59 mL/min/1.73m² were analyzed
Three models were compared: logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting
Performance used repeated cross-validation, calibration checks, subgroup analysis, and rule-out testing thresholds
infographic.evidence_signal: In 687 participants, all models showed similar modest discrimination (AUC about 0.72 overall), with weaker performance in people without diabetes.
infographic.watch_item: This was a survey-based observational analysis in a moderate CKD population, so the results may not generalize to other settings or replace direct urine albumin measurement in practice.
infographic.paper_title: Can Routine Clinical Variables Substitute for Urine Albumin Testing in Moderate Chronic Kidney Disease? A Machine Learning Analysis of NHANES 2015 to 2018

title: AI-Enabled Echocardiography Identifies Prominent Epicardial Adipose Tissue Associated With an Adverse Cardiometabolic Profile
authors: Aminorroaya, A.; Coppi, A.; McNamara, R. L.; Lima, J. A. C.; Krumholz, H. M.; Antoniades, C.; Khera, R.; Oikonomou, E. K.
abstract: BackgroundExcess epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) is associated with cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) dysfunction, but its assessment has traditionally required advanced imaging. ObjectivesWe investigated whether AI-enabled echocardiography could characterize epicardial adiposity and identify residual cardiometabolic risk beyond body mass index (BMI). MethodsWe developed PanAdipo, a video-based deep learning model in 1,114,441 videos from 28,797 studies across the Yale-New Haven Health System (YNHHS; 2016-2022), using report-derived expert reader labels of prominent EAT (2.3% of studies). PanAdipo was evaluated in five cohorts: a temporally distinct YNHHS transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) set (n=4,588 patients contributing 5,130 studies), an emergency department point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) cohort (n=10,957), the geographically distinct MIMIC-IV dataset (n=4,549), the community-based Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA Exam 6, n=2,740), and in held-out YNHHS patients with paired coronary CT angiography within 12 months (n=5,167). Analyses examined discrimination of the report label and of CT-defined high indexed EAT volume, correlation with paired cardiac CT phenotypes, and BMI-adjusted associations with cardiometabolic biomarkers and newly documented metabolic disease. ResultsIn the held-out health system test set, PanAdipo identified prominent EAT documented in clinical reports with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.86 (95% CI, 0.82-0.91) across all views and of up to 0.93 when combining apical 4-chamber and parasternal views. Against paired CT-derived measurements, PanAdipo discriminated age- and sex-specific high EAT (EAT/heart volume [≥]95th percentile) with AUROCs of 0.91 to 0.95 across age-sex groups and correlated more strongly with indexed EAT volume ({rho}=0.76) than with BMI ({rho}=0.41, all P<0.001); PanAdipo alone explained 53% of indexed EAT volume variance, versus 23% for age, sex, and BMI combined. In MESA, higher scores were associated with an adverse metabolic profile (higher HOMA-IR [{beta}=0.17 per SD; 95% CI, 0.11-0.22]) after adjustment for age, sex, and BMI. In health system TTE and POCUS cohorts, higher scores were associated with newly documented MASLD/MASH (BMI-adjusted HRpooled 1.31 [1.03-1.67] per SD of log[PanAdipo]) and hyperlipidemia (1.11 [1.04-1.18]). ConclusionsAI-enabled echocardiography provides a scalable digital biomarker that characterizes prominent epicardial adiposity and is associated with an adverse cardiometabolic profile, highlighting a role for echocardiography in metabolic risk stratification. CONDENSED ABSTRACTEpicardial adipose tissue (EAT) is linked to cardiometabolic risk, but its assessment has traditionally required advanced imaging. We developed PanAdipo, a deep learning model that derives a digital biomarker of EAT from routine echocardiography. PanAdipo tracks CT-defined epicardial adiposity ({rho}=0.76; AUROC 0.91-0.95 for age-/sex-specific high indexed-EAT), yet correlates modestly with body mass index (BMI; {rho}=0.19-0.41). After BMI adjustment, higher scores were associated with insulin resistance in a community-based cohort and newly documented metabolic disease across health systems. AI-enabled echocardiography may provide a scalable window into epicardial adiposity, with potential applications for enriching trial populations and monitoring response to cardiometabolic therapies.

infographic.key_insight: AI on routine echocardiography can spot prominent epicardial adipose tissue and flag residual cardiometabolic risk beyond BMI.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could turn standard heart ultrasound into a low-cost screen for hidden epicardial fat burden linked to adverse metabolic health.
method: Trained the video-based deep learning model PanAdipo on 1.11 million echo videos from 28,797 studies with expert report labels for prominent epicardial adipose tissue.
Validated performance across multiple external cohorts, including TTE, POCUS, MIMIC-IV, and MESA, plus paired cardiac CT angiography.
Compared AI scores with CT-derived epicardial fat measures, BMI, and metabolic biomarkers/disease outcomes.
infographic.evidence_signal: PanAdipo achieved AUROC 0.86 for report-labeled prominent EAT on held-out echo data, up to 0.93 with selected views, and 0.91-0.95 for CT-defined high EAT; it correlated more strongly with indexed EAT volume (rho=0.76) than BMI (rho=0.41).
infographic.watch_item: Because the model was trained and validated in retrospective datasets, real-world deployment still needs prospective testing, workflow integration, and attention to site-specific imaging quality.
infographic.paper_title: AI-Enabled Echocardiography Identifies Prominent Epicardial Adipose Tissue Associated With an Adverse Cardiometabolic Profile
